title: Stony Brook study: bot tested a deliberately exposed AWS key 7.86 seconds after publication
date_note: The page gives only its own publication day; the study's dates are not stated.
geo_basis: country; the page names Stony Brook University but no location
summary: Malwarebytes reports a Stony Brook University study that placed honeypot container images in eight public registries over four months. A bot tested a deliberately exposed AWS key 7.86 seconds after publication, the fastest use observed. The researchers say the decoys held working keys tied to monitoring so any use would show in provider logs.
plain: Researchers left fake-but-monitored cloud keys in public software registries. A bot tried one AWS key within about 8 seconds, according to Malwarebytes' account of the study.
exec: Malwarebytes reports that exposed cloud keys were tested within seconds in a university study, so a brief exposure can matter.
action: Malwarebytes advises that if a key was ever published, even briefly, you revoke it, replace it, and review account activity and charges.
impact: Research findings only; no real victim.

validation.note: Single publisher (Malwarebytes) relaying the Stony Brook study; the paper itself was not read.
